title: CRISPR: an adaptive immune system in bacteria, and a programmable cut

body:
## The mechanism the 2012 paper claims

Jinek, Chylinski, Fonfara, Hauer, Doudna, and Charpentier (Science, 2012) titled their paper "A Programmable Dual-RNA–Guided DNA Endonuclease in Adaptive Bacterial Immunity."

The title is the mechanism, compressed. Bacteria and archaea keep an adaptive immune system, CRISPR/Cas, aimed at foreign nucleic acids. In the type II system the paper studies, immunity uses two RNAs, not one: a CRISPR RNA and a trans-activating CRISPR RNA. The Crossref record's summary of the paper says both RNAs were required. The endonuclease they guide cuts DNA at a place the RNA sequence picks out. "Programmable" means the target is chosen by the guide sequence rather than by a new protein for every target.

## What this card will not inflate

**Fact:** that paper reports a dual-RNA-guided DNA endonuclease as part of bacterial adaptive immunity.

**Not a medical result:** editing a human disease, a clinic, or a safety record. Those are later uses and later arguments. The 2012 mechanism is a bacterial defense that turns out to be steerable.

**Not settled here:** every downstream ethical dispute about editing germline cells. The biochemistry of the bacterial system does not decide them.
